maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION
GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION

speechtext:
On the Orders of the Day:
SIR HENRY DRAYTON (West York):
I desire to refer to a matter that has already been brought to the attention of the House by my hon. leader (Mr. Meighen). It is a question that deeply involves the fair fame and good name of Canada, and for that reason I bring it forward again. I refer to the attack made by The Outlook on Canada and Canadian institutions. When the matter was before the House on the previous occasion, the Government took a position similar to that taken by the leader of the Opposition; but I regret that, apparently, they have not been able to make very much headway in dealing with it. I notice that The Outlook, ifar from desisting or apologizing, has returned to the charge, according to The Globe of Saturday, April 8. For the first time now we have an opportunity of studying this article. The Outlook is printed in London, I think, but I do not know anything regarding its standing, and I am perfectly convinced that both the British Government and the English people would just as much resent the attack made upon Canada as this House ought to resent it. I shall! read one or two paragraphs from the article, which has been widely distributed through the press of Canada.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION
speechtext: I do not know that the hon. member is strictly in order, but as the matter to which he refers seems to cast a reflection upon the honour of this country, I think it is of sufficient importance to warrant being brought 'before the attention of the House in order to elicit from the Government some statement regarding the facts. I would ask the hon. member, however, to refrain from reading any extract from the newspaper in question.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION
speechtext:
Instead of reading, I may point out that the newspaper states that it is now more than two years since the previous government, by daring and unscrupulous trickery, befooled the railway organisation into an arbitration. The publication attacks the standing

Grand Trunk Arbitration
of the gentlemen who took part in that arbitration, and it is utterly at variance with the truth when it claims that iSir Thomas White, who was one of the members of the board, was a member of the "inner ring" of the Meighen government. Of course, every hon. member knows that he had nothing to do with the Meighen government, but had resigned from the House, if I remember rightly, before Mr. Meighen assumed office.
The article further goes on to say that, notwithstanding the tremendous increase in the cost of railway operation, the Canadian Government, for the purpose of forcing this railway completely into its power, steadily refused to give any rate increase until the fifteen per cent increase was allowed in March 1918. Well, as hon. members know, and as the fact is, there was no refusal by the Government of any application for a rate increase, the whole matter being in the hands of the Railway Commission.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION
speechtext:
Order. I would ask
the hon. member to refrain from making any comment or argument. I understood that he wished simply to call the attention of the Government to some very libellous statements reflecting on the honour of Canada and of the Canadian Government which have appeared in the London press. Having done so, he can ask what is the attitude of the Government with regard to those statements, but he should not enter upon any argument or comment.

maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is what I am endeavouring to do. but it is rather a large field to cover. However, I will be as brief as possible. I want to point out to the Government that the effect of the article is, in the first instance, a libel not only upon Canada, not only upon the Government of that day and upon the present Government, not only upon Canadian tradition, but something which is still more reprehensible,-an evident attempt by indirect means through the press to force this country into an abandonment of its rights, a veiled threat that unless exactly what the financial press of London thinks ought to be done by this Government in regard to the Grand Trunk is done, no further moneys can be raised in England for the development of Canada.
Now, my submission to the Government, Mr. Speaker, is that this article and this propaganda constitute a direct contempt of court. And other means apparently having failed, I would ask the Government

as to whether or not they are taking proceedings for contempt of court against this newspaper or any other newspaper engaged in similar propaganda. We must bear in mind that the very issue which is dealt with by this newspaper is now before the Privy Council by the express consent of the Canadian Government.
I would further point out this:
Contempt of court by speech or writing may be scandalizing the court itself, or by abusing parties to actions, or by prejudicing mankind in favour of or against a party before the cause is heard.
I am reading from the laws of. England, not from Canadian laws. It is laid down by English cases that:
There cannot be anything of greater consequence than to keep the streams of Justice clean and pure, that parties may proceed with safety both to themselves and to their characters. Speeches or writings misrepresenting the proceedings of the court or prejudicing the public for or gainst a party are contempts. Nothing is more incumbent on courts of Justice than to preserve their proceedings from being misrepresented nor is there anything of more pernicious consequence than to prejudice the minds of the public against persons concerned as parties in causes before the cause is finally heard.
It is pointed out by a well-known authority on English law, that one of the most mischievous things you can have is trial by newspapers when a trial by one of the regular tribunals of the country is going on,-just what we are having in this case.
In view of the authorities, which are perfectly clear, I desire to ask the Government what action is proposed to be taken against the publishers of this article.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: GRAND TRUNK ARBITRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat surprised that my hon. friend should seek to give so much publicity to this matter. When it came up last week the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) took exception to an article in the same newspaper as reflecting upon the honour of this country. In reply I said that in so far as that article reflected upon the honour of this House or this Parliament, I placed myself in entire agreement with him. Clearly that states the position before the world to-day as to Canada's attitude. So far as the article reflects in any way upon any transaction of this Parliament, we give it no credence whatever. But when my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) suggests that we should enter into a controversy with any section of the British press, I fear he is going rather far afield.

Questions
I cannot see that any further action is necessary on the part of the Government than simply to repeat that in so far as this article reflects upon the honour of this House or Parliament, there is no hon. member who would countenance it for a moment. The article has been replied to in other newspapers, and I think the English public will judge the source from which this and similar articles emanate, and will be as ready to appreciate the truth as any one else. In a word, I think my hon. friend is unduly sensitive with regard to this particular subject.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg Centre) moved:
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be confined to Territories not included in any Province of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as there has already been some discussion regarding the work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, I presume it will not be necessary to deal at length with this resolution. I would point out that the original operations of the police were confined to unorganized territories and had to deal with questions affecting the pioneer settlers, and I think we all recognize that excellent work was done under the rather primitive conditions which then prevailed in the Canadian Northwest. However, after the war was over, there came a transformation in the character of that police force, and they were asked to do the work of looking after those suspected of being alien enemies, and also, a little bit later, to watch those suspected of fomenting sedition or of being connected with industrial disputes. I think, probably, enough was said the other day to illustrate that there has been what I think we might almost call an abuse of power in connection with the activities of the force. For example, literature was seized on general warrants. I know of one instance, which I may mention by way of illustration, in which a library belonging to a gentleman-now an alderman in the city of Calgary, a very estimable citizen there,-a library which he had brought out from the Old Country some years before, was seized by the Mounted Police. He has been unable to obtain any definite information with regard to what was done with his books, much less to have them returned, and I am credibly informed that some of these volumes are now in the library of the Mounted Police barracks at Calgary. Books that were seized at the time of the raids on the homes of workingmen in Winnipeg were burnt by the cart load in the public incinerator in Winnipeg. A teamster, a very religious man,
Mounted Police

rescued one of these books from the flames and brought it to me. It was a Life of Jesus. Curious that that should be one of the seditious documents taken presumably from the home of one of the workers. I know that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, during the war, entered a library at Regina and took out of that library a copy of Myers' "History of Canadian Wealth" a book which was widely circulated by the Grain Growers' Guide two or three years previously-a book written largely in the library of this Parliament. Its statements are supported by documentary evidence. I do not know whether it is considered undesirable for the people to know how these huge fortunes have been built up here in Canada.
I referred on a previous occasion to the surveillance that, according to the reports of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, has been maintained on labour activities. The Labour people throughout this country resent the fact that a police force is sent to spy upon their movements. I do not read that the police have ever been detailed to be present at the meetings of, we will say, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, or of the Bankers' Association, or of boards of directors of our railway companies, yet some of us might think that possibly these organizations are doing as much to stir up revolt in the minds of the common people of this country as the utterances of some obscure labour man in Prince Albert or Lethbridge. It is rather significant that, although there are so many men who have been demobilized in this country, the Government of Canada has had to pay for recruiting for this force in Great Britain. There is no doubt that the force has become one of the spending departments of the Government, nearly $4,000,000 being spent upon it last year. What province, 1 ask, really wants this force at the present time? I am quite sure that the provinces which I know best-Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta-are not very desirous of having it. The great majority of the people resent having the force within their provincial boundaries, and I am not at all sure that these eastern provinces have relished the idea of having a police force, operated from Ottawa, stationed in their various towns and cities. I hold in my hands a resolution adopted at a regular meeting of the Board of Directors of the Grand Army of United Veterans held at Toronto, February 11th, 1922, which reads:
Motion :-J. F. Marsh-J. Vallentlne, "That this Dominion Board forthwith make representa-
[Mr. Woodsworth.l
tion to the Hon. W. Mackenzie King. Premier of Canada, and his Government, requesting the advisability of demobilizing the Royal Mounted Police as at present constituted, as it is the decided opinion of this Board, after full investigation, that there is no further necessity for the services of Dominion Police in organized territory and recommend the re-organization of the Royal Canadian Northwest Mounted Police at its pre-war strength." Unanimously Carried.
I very well remember when the mounted police first came over the mountains to British Columbia, and the effect upon the workers there. We had a despatch from Ottawa stating that there would be demobilization of a very large number of returned men at the coast, that this might very likely mean unemployment, that unemployment would lead to industrial unrest, and hence that a detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were to be sent over the mountains to British Columbia. I think hon. gentlemen may imagine the feelings of the returned men at the coast when it was expressly stated to them that, since they, on their return, were likely to be out of a job, they were to be clubbed into submission by thte Mounted Police. Last year nearly $4,000,000 was spent on this police force, and only a little over half a million on unemployment relief. I think it would not be asking too much to suggest that these figures should be reversed, and that the larger amount should be spent in trying to relieve unemployment, rather than in being prepared to club the desperate unemployed into submission.
The last point which I make is that, after all, according to the division of functions in federal and provincial affairs, it has generally been considered that the administration of justice lay with the provinces and not with the federal authorities, and I take it that we would be proceeding on safe ground if we did not further centralize power in federal government with regard to the administration of justice. Those of us who knew anything of the inside of. the industrial dispute in Winnipeg in 1919 recognized very 4 p.m. clearly that it was a very dangerous precedent when the then Minister of Justice appointed a deputy minister in the city of Winnipeg and proceeded to administer justice within the province of Manitoba. My resolution calls for the placing of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on their pre-war basis. The force was organized to deal with conditions in unorganized territory where there was no proper police provision. Since that time the Canadian Northwest has been organized into provinces and each province now

Mounted Police
has its own provincial police force. I would urge upon this House that the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police be again restricted within the bounds of territories not yet organized into provinces.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Militia and Defence) : This is a much larger question than may appear on the surface. My hon. friend has referred to the pre-war basis of the Northwest Mounted Police. The House will understand that prior to 1920 Canada had two forces, one known as the Dominion Police and the other as the Northwest Mounted Police. In 1920 these two forces were amalgamated under the title of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They are, to all intents and purposes, at the present time, one force, but the Mounted Police proper does not comprise the full number of the men who now form the united organization. The passing by this House of a resolution demanding that the government restrict the activities of this force to the unorganized territories would hamper the government to a large extent in carrying out the policy which it hopes to make definite before many months. Speaking technically, on absolutely legal or constitutional grounds, my hon. friend is right that the provinces ought to look after the maintaining of order within their several territories. As I pointed out the other day, several of the prime ministers of the various provinces have suggested to the government that they do not go as far as this resolution would indicate, but that while agreeing to lessen the number of these forces, they would be loath to see the entire force of the Mounted Police withdrawn from their provinces, particularly from some parts of it. It is not easy just at the moment to take a definite stand as to these particular provinces. Even to-day I received a letter from the president of a board of trade in an important town in Ontario, begging me that, whatever else might be done, we should not withdraw the Mounted Police from that territorr and giving the reasons for it. I have a great many letters of this kind from mayors and private citizens. These are questions that we must carefully consider when the time comes for action in reference to this body knowm as the Mounted Police. I agree that constitutionally my hon. friend is absolutely right, but in working out the affairs, particularly of a new country, we
are not always safe in adhering to the letter of the constitution. Sometimes we even have to violate almost the letter of the law, in order to be practical. I think the most practical magistrate I ever knew in my life knew the least law of any magis. trate that had ever held office in Ontario. It was in a part of the country where every day common sense sometimes over-rode the law.
As to the amount of money spent on the Mounted Police, I can assure the house that the Government has in mind greatly reducing this amount of expenditure. We believe the time has come-and I think the House will agree with that conclusion'- when the force known as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police can be greatly reduced, and if parliament had not urged strongly that the management of this force should be taken out of the Militia Department, I had hoped to have some suggestion to make along that line; but the House having taken this attitude, we will have to begin over again, and it will take a little longer. I might take the House into my confidence to this extent, to say that I have asked Deputy Commissioner Starnes to suggest a plan for the reduction of his force in order to bring it nearer into conformity with the present-day need. I would assure my hon. friend and the House that, so far as practicable, we intend to confine the activities of the force to the unorganized territory, but in some instances the work Which I believe ought to be done will be greatly hampered if the House pass this resolution and tie the hands of the Government.

I referred the other day to this question, and I say that I entirely disagree with the principle laid down, that the administration of the law is a matter for the provinces. As the Dominion increases in importance and in subjects that are within its jurisdiction, it must maintain order, peace and good government throughout its area. I entirely dissent from the statement that the provinces are to be the interpreters of the rights and the duties of the federal government. The special officers of the Attorney General of the United States, backed by the thousands of special agents, under them, were in Washington throughout the whole of the Disarmament Conference, and were responsible for the maintenance of peace and order while that conference lasted. The President, the Attorney General, and all his attorneys in the United States are thor-
Mounted Police

oughly organized to preserve good government, and I should not be .surprised to see the President, before this week is over, take charge of the mines of the United States if the disturbances increase. In the early history of the American Union the responsibility rested mainly upon the states to see that peace and order were observed. But in the one hundred and fifty years' experience of that country the federal power has been gradually growing, the number of federal courts has increased, the number of officers necessary for the enforcement of federal law greatly added to, and more and more responsibility has been placed on the Attorney General through the hundreds of officers and local attorneys under him. The jurisdiction of the federal courts has also 'been gradually extended, and it has been found absolutely necessary to have not only attorneys, and local courts, but all the machinery essential for the proper enforcement of federal decrees. The same thing is coming in Canada. We have taken over the railways, and our federal laws concerning those railways cannot be properly administered except through the aid of a federal force. All through the war, whenever any consignment of money was entrusted to the express companies, there were always two members of the Mounted Police force to take charge of it. I have myself seen these escorts on trains coming into Ottawa. We have an Attorney General in Canada who is responsible for the administration of federal law, and in the Old Country there is an Attorney General for Scotland and one for Ireland.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service

There are no provincial governments there.
Mr. MACLEAN (York); Scotland and Ireland have their Attorneys General and local organizations. But here is the point: Scotland Yard is at the disposal of the Attorney General of either Scotland] or Ireland ,for the preservation of law and order in their respective territories. The more I observe the trend of things the more am I convinced of the necessity for a police force of some kind for the proper enforcement of federal law. There are thousands of officers now in the United States Who have been appointed for the sole purpose of enforcing the prohibition law; and so long as federal laws are being enacted, and new social problems connected with government are cropping up, the more responsibility will the federal power find itself compelled

to shoulder. I should not like to see the Minister of Justice, the Attorney General, or the Prime Minister of Canada without an efficient police force at his disposal. I do not propose for one moment to justify what has been done in cases that have provoked criticism, and for that reason I shall say nothing regarding the use of federal officers for putting the law into effect in Winnipeg during the strike; I shall say nothing regarding the requests of various people scattered throughout the Dominion for a federal force; nor will ,1 refer to the action of the federal force in the past. I do think, however, that there should have been more courage in the defence of the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) in advocating the maintenance of the force. I agree with him that it should1 be cut down in the interest of economy. But, I repeat, you cannot have a federal power without some kind of police force to Carry out its decrees. I do not suppose there were twenty federal officers in the United States in the early days of that country, but today there is an immense organization and secret service force at the disposal of the Attorney General, besides millions of money. If we in Canada desire to vindicate the British North America Act we must stand by the federal power and provide the necessary machinery to enforce the laws which the federal Parliament enacts. We have a Supreme Court, a Court of Exchequer, a Board of Railway Commissioners, and we have a minister in this House charged with the collection of customs duties and the putting down of smuggling and all illicit business of that kind. Let us, therefore, strengthen the hands of those who are charged with the enforcement of these laws. The provinces do not like to enforce federal laws, and there is the expense in connection therewith to be considered. The municipalities evade their responsibilities in 'some cases, and to-day in Ontario we find Mr. Drury putting through the legislature a law for the establishment of a provincial police with men scattered throughout the province for the enforcement of provincial law. That is only another form of the same problem we have here. If you undertake the responsibility, as the federal authority, of enforcing the decrees of your courts, you have also to assume the responsibility of maintaining peace and order and good government, if the provincial authorities fail to undertake that responsibility; and especially you have to assume this responsibility now in view of

Mounted Police
the great developments along these lines which have taken place in the United States. I have already referred to the precautions taken by the United States Government while the Conference for Disarmament was being held in Washington, to prevent bombing outrages or any other attempts to disturb its proceedings. As a result of a long-drawn-out legal fight between the federal and state authorities, the States Rights party of the United States has absolutely broken down for all time.
That is the situation in the United States, and we are reaching pretty much the same state of affairs here. While I do not dispute what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Woodsworth) has said with regard to recent strikes, I do not think he has made out a case against the continued maintenance of the mounted police for the preservation of peace, order and good government. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) has not had the courage to state what his views are in relation to this question. But he must know that some such force is absolutely necessary for the purposes I have enumerated, and that it should be under the administration of either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) referred to the strike of 1919. In my judgment what happened there in that year is the best argument that can be advanced for the maintenance of the Mounted Police as an efficient force to uphold law and order. Let us recall for a moment what took place there. An incipient revolution broke out; the municipal authorities were unable to control the situation; the men who planned the revolution had the local police under their control-they went on strike. The provincial authorities were unable to restore order, and if it had not been for the Mounted Police and for the action taken by the federal authorities, we would have had Soviet government in Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member " doth protest too much." He is too sensitive on that particular point.

Mounted Police

I want to argue for the continuance of the Mounted Prfliee as an efficient federal force, and, that the recent history of this country proves that the continuance of that force is absolutely necessary; and I referred to what took place in the city of Winnipeg in 1919 to confirm my argument.
As the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) has pointed out, a very large part of the work of this force is that of secret service. Perhaps my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg would say there is no necessity for a secret service; but looking over some of the events that have happened lately, I think such a service is essential, and if we are to have a secret service, what better type of men could one assign to it than the men who have been trained in the traditions of the Northwest Mounted Police? There is a force that throughout its history has won the confidence, respect and admiration not only of the people of this country, but of other countries as well, especially of the United States, where the administration of justice has come in comparison with the administration of justice in the Dominion. To confine the activities of this force to the Arctic Circle would be a very grave mistake, and I think it is absolutely necessary to have on hand as an efficient secret service, and as a force that can give the requisite service in cases of emergency, this Mounted Police force.
When my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg assumes to speak for Labour in this country, I do not think that he is representing it at all. He certainly is not representing what is known as international trades unionism, the only sane kind of unionism that we have in this country. I am an advocate of international trades unionism because it believes in the fulfilment of contracts,- they were the men in the city of Winnipeg who were forced by their international office to go back and keep the contracts that they had entered into. I say that labour operated under principles of that kind will strengthen the position of the workingmen, make him respected all over Canada, and give him a place and standing in the community that he can never have if he runs wild and follows the lead of Red agitators.

speechtext:
Just before the question is put, I would like to draw my hon. friend's attention to a point which may possibly have escaped his notice and also the notice of the House. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be confined to territories not included in any province of Canada.
In proposing this motion, the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg1, (Mr. Woods-worth) has, no doubt, regarded the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as being identical with the old Royal Northwest Mounted Police. If so, I should inform him that two years ago, by Act of this Parliament, the nature and complexion of the force was considerably changed. The name was changed from "Royal Northwest Mounted Police" to "Royal Canadian Mounted Police"; and subsequently, under certain powers conferred on the Governor-inCouncil by statute, the Dominion Police were welded in as part of the Royal Canadian Police. To-day, therefore, what was the old Dominion Police, the men who amongst other duties have to do with the policing of Parliament Hill and the Government buildings, are part of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and if the resolution were to be carried in its present form the police who appear round these

Mounted Police
buildings would under its terms have to be abolished. I may say to my hon. friend that there were a good many who expressed doubt as to wisdom of the course the Government of the day was nursing in changing the headquarters of the Mounted Police to Ottawa and merging the old Dominion Police with the new organization.
As the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) explained this afternoon, the Government has under consideration certain changes in regard to this force. Many of us are strongly of the view that the old Dominion Police should be distinct altogether from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and that is one of the matters under consideration in connection with the readjustment of these forces. With that explanation, I think my hon. friend's purpose may have been served in the discussion which we have had. I do not think the motion should be allowed to carry in its present form without the House understanding that it would abolish the forces used for Dominion Police purposes, as well as those used in the provinces for the purposes of the Mounted Police generally.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I find myself in general sympathy with the purpose of this resolution, although I cannot by any means agree with some of the arguments that my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has advanced in support of it. I stated my position on this question the other day when the bill of the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) to amalgamate the defence arms of Canada was before the House. I wish briefly to re-state that position: I consider it is no part of the business of the federal government to do police work in the provinces, and it is on that ground that I think the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be confined to the unorganized territories. I agree with the view expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King)-well, I shall not refer to it as his view, because I did not understand that he expressed it as the opinion of the Government; but it is my view-that the Dominion Police that formerly did the work of policing the Government buildings and carried out the secret service work of the Government, should be dissociated from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and restored to the position it formerly occupied.
The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has argued, with his usual vigour, that the federal government should make provision for federal enforcement of
53i
federal laws. That was not the understanding at the time the Dominion of Canada was formed; the enforcement of law was left to the provinces; and I think there it should remain. As to the part played by the Northwest Mounted Police in the Winnipeg strike or in connection with the other troublous periods through which we have passed, no blame can attach to them, for they simply carried out orders. The police must always carry out orders given to them by those charged with the responsibility of seeing that the law is enforced. I am not arguing on the merits or demerits of the Winnipeg case; I merely wish to lay that down as the consideration that should govern in the matter.
The item of expense is a very considerable one. We are asked to vote this year almost $3,000,000 for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and in view of this circumstance-I express my own personal view alone-I submit that the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, as they are ordinarily understood, should be confined to the unorganized territories and that the Dominion Police should be re-established to do the work that they have always done around Ottawa and as well the secret service work of the Government.
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) raised the point that a police force of this kind was necessary to maintain law and order, to meet emergencies such as, he said, existed in Winnipeg in 1919-although my own view is that he has somewhat overdrawn the picture in respect to that occasion. But we had the means of meeting such emergencies before the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were located at Ottawa; the militia of Canada could be called out to maintain law and order in such cases, if the municipal or provincial authority was unable to do so. I do not like the idea of developing the notion throughout this Dominion that the federal government should be charged with the enforcement of law that hitherto has rested in the provinces alone.

speechtext:
I do not think it is necessary to debate the resolution very much particularly as there has been no very serious objection offered to it. The position of the Government, as it has been expressed, is towards the object of the resolution, I gather. I am also in agreement with the statement that has been made by the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Crerar).
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), however, presumed to state a case to the House and endeavoured to prove the absolute necessity for this particular force being retained in its present function and control. As that has been the only argument that has been advanced against the resolution, it might be well for me simply to point out-although I do not think it is really necessary, because I am sure the House saw for itself-that the hon. member failed absolutely to establish his case. He did tell us that there was an incipient revolution at Winnipeg at a certain time, but he failed entirely to prove it. I think I am as near the truth when I say there was no incipient revolution in Winnipeg, and still nearer the truth when I say that the trouble in Winnipeg, so far as prolonging the disorder was concerned, was actually due to the action of the Mounted Police. Therefore I claim that the point that the hon. member for West Toronto attempted to make was not established at all. His boasting about his ability to get votes may have some bearing on this subject, although I must confess I fail to see what, but inasmuch as he has introduced that point, I might say that it is not a conclusive proof of the intelligence of the men of the labour movement at Toronto that they should give the hon. member more votes than anybody else. I have my doubts, however, about his endor-sation by the organized labour movement of that city and their anxiety to get votes for him. I have the honour to be one of the representatives of the organized labour movement of Canada, that sane labour movement to which he refers, and I believe that that sane labour movement would concur in the spirit of the resolution before the House, that there is no necessity for duplicating our forces, but that, on the other hand, it would probably lead to much conflict between the provincial and Dominion authorities, and that it would be better that the Mounted Police should fulfil its function of policing the territories that are not now under the provincial government.

One more thing and I am through. The hon. member for West Toronto also made another wise statement. He said that he knew of a great number of people who wanted to do away with all police whatsoever. If he knows people of that kind, they must be in Toronto; I do not know anywhere else where they could be. I want to dissociate myself from any such people. We recognize, of course, the necessity for maintaining law and order, and are just as ready to see that that is done as my hon. friend. There is no implication in this resolution that police forces should be eliminated. The resolution merely seeks to define what shall be the real function of this force, whether it shall be continued as ' a spy system on the labour forces of this country, or whether it shall be confined to its original and proper function of policing the unorganized territories of Canada.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I have listened to the debate with a great deal of interest. The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) have, of course, a full right to their opinions and to their expression in this House, and I hope that they will accord to me and others the same privilege. I have lived in the West for twenty-three years and have seen quite a bit of the workings of the Northwest Mounted Police out there, having been a justice of the peace for a few years. I cannot agree with my friends who are representing Labour in this House in the accusations they have made against the Northwest Mounted Police. I have seen those men abused when they were trying to carry out their duty, but I have never seen them fail in the discharge of their duty. I have never seen them oppress people. I have seen them handled pretty rough and when they have had to fight back, but I think any man who is worth anything will fight back when he has to. I think the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg is prejudiced against the force because of his experience with it during the Winnipeg strike. My hon. friend says that there was no incipient revolution at Winnipeg. Now I have a card here that was issued at the time of the Winnpeg strike, and I want to read it so that everybody can judge for himself as to the nature of that movement. It was issued to the lumber camps throughout British Columbia and is the same as was issued in Winnipeg, I am told. It reads as follows:

Mounted Police
Workers!
Your recent fight by means of the "strike" to secure an eight-hour day and better working conditions has failed. You know the reason. Lack of courage on the part of some mill men and the importation of scabs-spineless creatures. However, there is no need to be discouraged as the fight is not yet lost- You have another weapon, and a good one, sabotage. Lay down on the job. Sabotage by a hundred and one tricks resulting in the withdrawal of efficiency. You can win and kick the boss in the ribs at the same time.
The real loggers are leaving the G.T.P. and the boss can not make out with prairie chickens.
That was the name for the homesteaders who took the place of the strikers. It goes on:
Lay down on the job!
In a short time the boss will realize that it is better to give eight hours, dean camps, better conditions and good food all round and thus get the real loggers to stay, than to mush around with prairie chickens and bush-whacking homesteaders.
Lay down on the job !
Get fired. What of it? You don't own that job. It is lent to you only so long as you produce profits for the boss.
Lay down on the job!
It is your most potent weapon. Go to it. Most of the bosses along the line are not worth 30 cents. Bust'em! The one you can't bust you can get fired. Hutton for instance.
That is where I picked up this card.

speechtext:
The card goes on:
Lay down on the job. Sabotage !
Ask your fellow worker how the woods and mill mens' strike was won in Washington, Idaho, in 1917. Lay down on the job. Workers of the world, unite. You have nothing but your chains to lose and the whole world to gain.
Now those men were threatening to burn the sawmill with the consequent destruction of a million dollars worth of property, and we had to use force to quell the disturbance. We could not get the provincial police, we could not get the Mounted Police-they were all busy. I have quoted this card to show hon. members that this was an attempt at breaking down that law and order which most of us are standing up for and whose observance we are trying to maintain. It is all well enough to say that the local authorities can deal with a
situation when it arises; but I agree with the hon. member from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) that there are times when the Mounted Police can control disorder much more efficiently than the local police, and they have done it on many occasions.
My hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg said that most of the people do not want the Mounted Police. I do not know on what foundations he bases his claim to speak for the majority of the people, or where he obtains the evidence that they sympathize with his view. I think they do want the Mounted Police. There were four millions spent in 1921 on the force the hon. gentleman says, and less than half a million on employment doles. Well, it is too bad we have to spend such a sum as four millions, but as long as there are such disorders as those to which I have referred I would be willing to spend twice that amount in order to maintain order. I am friendly to Labour but I am not in sympathy with them when they take such a course as I have pointed out. I am a Labour man and to some extent a capitalist too; but I have to work and I would like the little money I have to earn something too. I do not want conditions to prevail under which there would be no security for a man's home or his business.
In Winnipeg, during the strike, defiance of law and order were manifested. The operation of public services of all kinds was stopped and there was even interference with the delivery of milk to the hospitals. If such a thing as that does not constitute a hardship for poor people I do not know the real definition of the term. -1 think the labour people have been very poorly led. If I -submitted to the leadership of others for twenty-five years and at the end of that time found myself penniless whilst those leaders were in comfortable circumstances I would think I had been misled. To my mind the gentlemen who have been speaking for Labour are not in reality Labour's true friends; they are mistaken in the methods they advocate for curing the evils of which they complain. Most of us wish to see better conditions brought about for labour-most of us indeed labour ourselves-but there is a proper way to bring about that improvement. To protest against the police and to abuse them-and I am sorry to say that some critics are all too prone to follow that course-will never result in improved conditions. I think it is far easier to get those in authority to listen to reason than
Mounted Police

ignorant labouring men such as are engaged in fomenting strikes of the character described. Personally, I stand for the maintenance of the Mounted Police in Canada.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I represent the constituency described in this resolution as "territory not included in any province of Canada," and I propose to speak to this motion although it is not of so much importance to me as it is to members representing provincial constituencies. As a Canadian, and as a resident of British Columbia, I wish to say that I would be very sorry indeed to see the Royal Cana-' dian Mounted Police removed from that province. It is admitted I think, even by the mover of the present resolution, that the force should not be removed from unorganized territories. Having resided, for the past twenty years in a territory where there was no other police force than the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, I can speak with experience when I say that that force, at all times and under all circumstances, has discharged its duty in a manner which merits hearty commendation rather than criticism or abuse. The Northwest Mounted Police, as has already been said this afternoon, has excited the admiration not only of Canadians but of people throughout the length and breadth of the world as an efficient and admirable force. My experience of their conduct has been gained as a citizen and from practice in the courts where I have assisted, or have opposed, the police in various prosecutions; and I can say without hesitation that on all occasions they have conducted themselves in a manner that is above criticism. Even in cases where the evidence in their possession showed the accused to be a criminal they have invariably acted with perfect fairness; and I have never seen them hesitate to bring forward evidence tending to indicate innocence as well as evidence pointing to guilt-their submission of cases in the courts has been invariably characterized by fairness. After such an experience of the conduct of the force as that I am bound say that when I hear undeserved criticisms directed at the force it excites a suspicion in me as to the reason for such action. If we have in this Dominion forces that would upset legally constituted authority, or would proceed in other than a constitutional and legal way, and a Dominion force is required to prevent their activities I say that the operations of the Mounted 
Police should be continued throughout the length and breadth of Canada. After all, who is the best judge as to whether this force is needed or not? I say the Government of the day is the best qualified to pronounce upon that point; and if the Government, after advice from the Department of Justice, feels that it requires this force it is perfectly justified in maintaining it. Furthermore I have not the slightest doubt that if any one province of Confederation intimated to the federal authorities that the presence of the Mounted Police was distasteful the Dominion government would not hesitate one moment in removing the force from that province. I think the question can very well be left in the hands of the Government of the day regardless of what its political views may be. The Mounted Police throughout all the years of its existence has not been administered in the interests of any particular party. It has been the same fine force, all through the years of its history, regardless of the political views of those at the head of affairs of the Dominion, and I say we can very well leave this matter in the hands of the Government of the day. If the federal government thinks it needs the force it will continue it: if it thinks the force is not required it will remove it or cut its strength down to the number required. Personally I believe it would be unwise to handicap any government by passing such a resolution as this at the present time.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I was in Winnipeg during the strike to which allusion has been made this afternoon and I think I can give unprejudiced testimony as to what happened. Living four hundred miles from that city and being there at the time on a visit I was not in the same inflamed state of mind as perhaps some of the parties to the controversy were. I want to say for the information of those who got their impressions of what occurred at that time through the press, that the disturbance in Winnipeg was subsequent to the action taken by the Mounted Police and not prior to it. As an unprejudiced, and I hope fair-minded, witness. I believe sincerely that there would have been no disturbance whatever had the Mounted Police not intervened.
I was in Winnipeg for two days, which included the time of the strike, and I never missed a single meal. I enjoyed all the comforts of life during that period, and I

Mounted Police
never perceived at any moment anything like an incipient revolution. I agree with the statement of the labour member from Winnipeg, when he says that the labour men are not of the type that would be implied from the speech of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken). These men are so much in earnest that they sometimes become extremists, yet I believe they belong to the type of sane labour representatives. I desire to give my personal testimony at this time to that effect. I am speaking without any prejudice. I have never had any association with labour and never in contact with it, and view it without prejudice of any kind. I always feel, however, that I must be on the side of the under dog. To that extent, perhaps, I am a little biased. I want the members of this House to disabuse themselves of the idea that was propagated by the newspapers that there was anything like a Soviet revolution in Winnipeg, because such was not the case.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with the sentiment expressed by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird). Although he has not spoken from real experience of labour conditions, I may say that I can speak from such experience to a certain extent. In my younger days I had something to do with labour organizations, and was among the actual labourers and realizing and knowing the conditions which are forced upon one, there is a memory and sting left that will never be removed, and until men live through these conditions and realize them, they will not know the story, and should not stand up in this House as authorities upon the subject. They must have the experience before they can speak on these matters. The hon. member for Nelson referred to the strike in Winnipeg, which was magnified by the press report. There was little trouble before the red uniform of the Mounted Police was seen on the streets of Winnipeg, with the avowed object of suppressing whatever movement was on foot, whether the movement had any justification or not. I state further that I believe it was the propaganda of the government of the day. At the time of the revolution, or of the trouble, in Winnipeg-revolution, so called by the papers-we were sitting in Regina, an organized body of farmers, who were supposed to be the authors and finishers of another Soviet or Bolshevist movement, according to the sentiments advertised and
expressed throughout the country 5 p.m. by the then government and word came to eighty-five of us, who were an executive representing the various electoral districts of Saskatchewan, "For God's Sake hold firm." That was the word that came to the executive who sat in Regina at that time. Oh yes, the government of the day were frightened. I might recall to the minds of the members who sat in this House two years ago the fact that the then hon. member for Calgary, when this or a similar question was being discussed, rose in his place, and said "What would this country do if red revolution broke out"? That was the sentiment behind the government when they brought into force the amalgamation or co-ordination of the Mounted Police and Dominion Police as explained by the present Minister of Militia and Defence, (Mr. Graham). I want to state that if the present Government is following out that principle, or accepting it as a principle, I do not agree with it. Further than that I recollect that when the debate which I have just mentioned took place in this House two years ago hon. gentlemen who now constitute the Government were rising in this Chamber and endorsing the principles as outlined in this resolution, but there is silence to-day and I think the country will ask the question: Where is the consistency? The knitted brows of the earnest workers are no longer in evidence. Where is it now? Do they believe or have they lost faith? That is the question as I see it.
I might state that I have lived in that western country for 31 years. I have been in close association with the Mounted Police. I have known of their activities. They are human. The human element enters into them as well as all others. They are a body of men who individually and collectively will go out into the waste areas of the West and they will bring in the recreant or Indian. They will go out into the vast country alone, being away months, they will perform great feats of valour, but I say that history will record a distinct mark between the time of the amalgamation of the two forces. The old Northwest Mounted Police do not like to hand down the traditions which they erected as a body, and let the newly organized force share with them the halo and glory which is theirs. This new force has to establish a record before the old Northwest Mounted Police will allow the glamour and glory that attached to the old force
Mounted, Police

to be shared by the present organization. I believe that as a body of men they should be again organized under the old name, with the same work to do. Whether in organized territories or whether under provincial jurisdiction or new jurisdiction, those men will go back and perform the work the authorities ask of them.
The old Northwest Mounted Police-I have heard them express this sentiment many times-do not wish to be incorporated with a body of men who have to go into urban centres and suppress disturbances, because their conception was that they were established, as I have related, to go into the wider areas, to hunt what might be termed the horse-thief or the recreant, or even the Eskimo, to administer justice and to keep order. That is why the term " mounted " was applied to them. They have done their work well. I think there is a work to be performed yet in that regard, and my sentiment would be that the unorganized territories of this vast country alone require police of that nature. I think that another force of a Dominion character might be created in this country, but do not associate them with the old Northwest Mounted Police.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I think it is very unfortunate that we have had two questions confused. It will be very difficult for some of us to vote intelligently on this matter, in view of the confusion of these two issues. I think, as the Prime Minister pointed out, that probably the resolution is more far-reaching than the mover intended, and I believe it would be in the interests of all concerned that it should be withdrawn. If there was a resolution that was directed against some of the orders that were issued to the Mounted Police in those days I would myself heartily support it. I think, however, it might be well if this House would forget some of the things that happened in war time. There was a spirit of hysteria abroad. Undoubtedly the Mounted1 Police had duties committed to them that were not pleasant for them to perform. I may say that the present police force has some duties committed to it that are rather degrading to a police force. The suppression of race track gambling is degrading to such a force. If we could clearly separate the two issues that are placed before us, I think it would be very much easier to vote intelligently on this resolution. For my part I have no hesitation in condemning some of the

orders that were issued to the police. As I said, things were done that would reflect no credit on those responsible for the issuing of the orders in those days. But just at the present time it is not possible for us clearly to distinguish between those who were responsible for issuing the orders and those who were charged with the responsibility of carrying them out. I should not like now to cast any reflections on the Mounted Police as such. Undoubtedly they did things which were disagreeable and distasteful to them; but I submit that in view of the confusion of those two issues it would not be possible for us to vote intelligently and I think the resolution should be withdrawn.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St John and Albert) :
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I
am not sure that in the interests of the country it is well to have the resolution withdrawn. It is perhaps as well for the chamber to take a vote and to stand up either for the Reds or against them. In the course of this debate there have been some expressions from hon. gentlemen which, whether so intended or not, were in my judgment nothing more or less than a simple pandering to the forces that seek to disorganize our social conditions as they exist. It is not a question of three or four million dollars; we can deal with that on the Estimates, as also with the question as to the number of the men and their location, It is not a question of. administration, because the force could be administered separately from the other branch of the force, the Dominion Police, as we know them. I believe we had better go straight to the part of the resolution that is simply intended to emphasize a remark that fell from an hon. member recently, that the rioters in Winnipeg rioted because of the sight of a Mounted Police uniform. In the name of all that is common sense, what reason has a decent British subject, a Canadian subject, to revolt or riot at the sight of His Majesty's uniform? I do not know any decent, law-abiding citizen or man who ought to be outside a gaol who would find good cause, in the appearance of that uniform, for rushing into riot, fray, revolt, or any other species of law breaking. Let us have no pandering to those who would subvert our social organisation. Treat the resolution in the sense in which it is intended, to withdraw the forces, which are capable of protecting organized, peaceable, decent society, from the places where they can combat riot, revolution and disintegration. That is the question, and I

Mounted Police
shall have much pleasure, and feel I am doing my duty, in voting straight against any such proposition.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CONFINE TO UNORGANIZED TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I cannot very well see my way to withdraw the resolution. It seems to me that the dicussion has been extended much more widely than the resolution itself would justify. A good deal has been said with regard to the Winnipeg strike, which was introduced incidentally by myself. I do not very much blame hon. members who have referred to the strike for the way in which they have done so, because I know the information that went out through the press at the time. Those of us who live in Winnipeg, whether members of labour organizations or not, learned in the course of the long-drawn-out trials, how false those newspaper representations were. I may be permitted to call attention to the fact that I myself was one of the men charged with sedition at that time. And I was returned to Parliament not from a purely labour constituency by any means, but from Centre Winnipeg itself, which was represented here last year by Major Andrews, and I received a majority of some 3,740 over the man nearest to me. That in itself, I think, is sufficient to refute a great many of the charges that have been made by hon. gentlemen who have lived at a distance and have not known the details of the events in Winnipeg. As to the character of the charges that were made at that time, and the tactics pursued by those who were prosecuting, I do not think I can do better than quote one charge of sedition made against me personally. I shall read one count only, and you will see how Red I am:
The Jurors aforesaid do further present:
4. That J. S. Woodsworth, in or about the month of June, in the year of Our Lord One Thousand Nine Hundred and Nineteen, at the City of Winnipeg, in the Province of Manitoba, unlawfully and seditiously published seditious libels in the words and figures following:
"Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed; to turn aside the need from judgment, and to take away the right from the poor of my people, that widows may be their prey and that they may rob the fatherless.
"Isaiah (10: 1-2)"
"And they shall build houses and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for as the days of a tree are the days of my people, and mine elect shalfl long enjoy the work of their hands.
"Isaiah II (65 : 21-22)."
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to be the only man in the history of British
court procedure who has been charged with sedition for quoting from the King James version of the English Bible. I read this charge simply because it would be incredible to any one who was not familiar with the viciousness of the attack which was made upon labour people at that time, and with the misrepresentations which were circulated throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Labour men were charged with conspiracy. I think that one of these days we shall be in a position to show where the real conspiracy was. I have ventured to speak even thus far with regard to this question simply because there has been in the past either no representation, or a very slight representation, of the labour position on the floor of the House, and I think that is one reason why the country at large has been so misled regarding the real aims of labour.
The charge has been made that some of us do not represent International Labour. I may say that the only labour organization with which I was ever connected, and from which I received a withdrawal card, was the International Longshoremen's Association, Local 38-52. I would ask the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) whether he is in as close touch with labour as that. 1 do not know, I merely mention it. The political end of the labour organizations is in most cases entirely distinct from the industrial end. So it is natural that we do not represent some particular craft; we come here to represent the great body of labour. I think the fact that we are here surely gives us the right to speak on the floor of this House for at least a section of labour.
I would call attention to this fact, too, which is not generally understood: that it was the president of the Trades and Labour Council (International) of Winnipeg who gave the strike order; it was the secretary of that council who sent out that strike order. These men were then Internationals, they are Internationals still. At the time that strike was ordered there was no thought that it was anything else than an International movement, although undoubtedly there had been a movement towards the formation of a more efficient organization.
I might say further in regard to that strike-into details of which I have no thought of entering-that the trials clearly showed that while there were charges of an attempt to set up a Soviet government, an attempt at revolution by force of arms, yet notwithstanding all the searches of the
Mounted Police

Mounted Police from coast to coast the authorities failed to discover one single gun. Labour men may be fools, but certainly if they had intended an armed revolt one would suppose that they would have had at least a few guns in their possession. Nothing could have been further from the thoughts of these men. I say most emphatically that that strike arose as an industrial dispute over questions of higher wages and an interpretation of the principle of collective bargaining. It is quite true that under the old law of conspiracy-which had been almost obsolete in Great Britain for a hundred years, and which admitted a very wide range of evidence,-the procedure dating back to the Star Chamber days-it is quite true, I say, that under that almost obsolete law six of the men on trial were committed to gaol. But I would point out that there was such a revulsion of public opinion in the city of Winnipeg that the day these men were liberated three of them walked into the provincial legislature of Manitoba. Another man charged, Mr. F. J. Dixon, the leader of the Labour group in the Manitoba House, was given the most overwhelming majority ever accorded to any man in the city of Winnipeg. Surely this is evidence sufficient to show that the great mass of the people were misled as to the real character of that strike.
I do not know that any connection at all was shown by the hon. member between the document he read, purporting to emanate from the lumber camps of British Columbia, and the Winnipeg strike; hence it is not necessary to discuss its contents.
I confess that this matter is somewhat involved, as the Prime Minister has shown. The Dominion Police force was amalgamated with the Royal Canadian Northwest Mounted Police, it is true; but we have to deal with the situation as it is to-day, we have to deal with the Canadian Mounted Police. Now, my resolution would confine the activities of that particular force, as now constituted, to the unorganized territories. If it is found wise by the Department of Justice that a new Dominion police force should be organized, that can be done, but that does not interfere with the policy with regard to this force. So I think we must decide on the policy to be adopted by the people in relation to this matter.
The very attitude taken by some hon. members is what influences me very strongly to plead that this force should not again be used as it has been used in

the past. The fact is that Labour has been misunderstood and spied upon, and that in industrial disputes armed force has been used to quell labour opposition. The hon. Minister of Militia called attention to the fact that he had resolutions from certain boards of trade advancing reasons-which he did not give-why this force should be retained. Well, I can very readily understand that the Winnipeg Board of Trade most decidedly would advance reasons why the Mounted Police should be retained. It was the representative of the Citizens' Committee-a body which was really a creature of the Board of Trade-who was at the time of crisis appointed Deputy Minister of Justice. The House will appreciate the resentment of labour when the man who all along had been acting as spokesman for the Citizens' Committee

the employers' committee- was suddenly clothed with extraordinary powers to administer " impartial " justice. There was the difficulty, and it was that action which provoked resentment in the minds of labour towards the administration of justice at that time.
I would call attention to the fact that, although it has been stated that an attempt was made to set up a Soviet republic, yet, at that very time negotiations were being carried on between the provincial government and the workers, and had it not been for the precipitate action of the Mounted Police, or the authorities that ordered out the Mounted Police, we would not have had that shooting in the streets of Winnipeg. This is the reason why we should have another way of dealing with such a situation. The fundamental difficulty at that time was that an industrial strike had arisen on a larger scale than ever before had been known in this country. If a Soviet was established in the Labour temple-I say, if-if a body there assumed somewhat larger powers than it should have done, there was also another Soviet in the board of trade rooms which had also assumed governmental powers. In this contingency the municipal and provincial authorities stood helpless. The federal authorities remained inactive until a crisis developed, and then they came in with a club and made things all the worse. That was really the situation.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I would plead that we have reached a point in the history of Canada where industrialism has developed to such an extent that we shall have to deal with these disputes as they

Mounted Police
arise, not by brute force but rather by reasonable methods-when	instead of
spending $4,000,000, as has been suggested, in order to crush labour, if necessary, I would say: Let us rather spend $4,000,000 in studying this problem and in placing our industrial relations upon such a basis that we will have no need to call in the Mounted Police to settle any of these disputes. To-day we face the need for reconstruction, and I plead with the members of the Government to give us a lead along these lines. The Prime Minister has already in his book, Industry and Humanity, outlined some of the principles which might, if adopted, prove a solution. I do not know that we all agree with his proposed solutions; but I say: Let us give those principles a chance, and let us in any case seek to do this work in a constructive fashion.
But, after all, this is rather beside the original purpose of the resolution. We are past the war period; we are, I hope, past the period of hysteria inspired by the war. With the provinces thoroughly organized, I do submit we ought to be in a position to revert to the previous arrangements, and to confine the activities of this force as it now exists to the unorganized territories. I firmly believe that we are on good constitutional grounds, as the Minister cf Militia (Mr. Graham) admits, when we say that the administration of justice should be left with the provincial authorities. If they find at any time that there is a situation which they cannot control, it is then for them to call in the aid of the military authorities, not before. The ver^ presence of a body of this character, is, as I stated the other day, an irritant. I think I can speak for a very large number cf labour people at least when I say that if this force were taken out of this work of espionage, of this work by which they enter the homes of workingmen and seize literature, by which they act as agents provocateurs, it would go a long way toward establishing a better condition of affairs in the industrial life of Canada.
